body.heading: A mountain built by hand
paragraphs: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu. It contains roughly 2.3 million blocks of stone, many weighing more than a family car, and originally stood about 147 metres tall — the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.

Its sides align closely with the compass points, and its base is level to within a few centimetres across an area the size of several football fields. The builders achieved this with ropes, sighting tools, water levels and extraordinary patience.

body.heading: Who did the building?
paragraphs: Old stories claimed vast armies of enslaved people, but archaeology tells a different story. Excavations have uncovered a workers' town beside the pyramids, with bakeries, breweries and cemeteries where builders were buried with honour near the kings they served.

The evidence suggests teams of Egyptian labourers, many of them farmers working during the season when the Nile flooded their fields, organised into named crews that even left cheerful graffiti in hidden chambers. It was hard work — skeletons show the strain — but it was the work of a proud, well-fed workforce.

body.heading: The honest mystery: the ramps
paragraphs: How the blocks were raised is still debated. Straight ramps, zigzag ramps and spiral ramps have all been proposed, and the truth may combine several methods. We know stones arrived by boat along the Nile — a foreman's diary, the oldest inscribed papyrus found, records one team's journeys hauling limestone to Giza.
The pyramids are not a mystery beyond understanding. They are something better: proof of what organised, skilled, ordinary people can build when a whole society pulls together.

takeaway: The Great Pyramid was raised by organised Egyptian crews using boats, sledges, ramps and remarkable surveying — human skill, not magic.
